findings.F1: The check failed on Calmar alone (0.57 against 0.75): the book made +25.2 % a year over 7.94 years, but its deepest fall was −44.3 %. That fall lasted 213 days across windows w5–w6, starting in 2023. The book lost 0.26 % a day in it while the coins' daily returns summed to +26 %, so this fall is the fade losing, not the coins falling.
findings.F2: Every window had a fall from peak of at least 10 %, and nine windows had falls deeper than 30 % (w3, w4, w6, w7, w8, w9, w10, w12, w13, w14 range from −31 % to −44 %). The book was in a position on 98 % of coin-days, because a 24-hour hold is re-entered at each 00:00 bar. It therefore carries every case, including the weak ones.
findings.F3: The gain per case rises steeply with the size of the settlement-hour move. By quintile of |forecast| (about 3,404 independent cases each), the mean 24-hour fade return was +0.15 % (t 1.99), +0.13 % (t 1.46), +0.21 % (t 2.62), +0.41 % (t 4.87) and +0.63 % (t 6.31). The two weakest quintiles earn less than the 0.19 % a trade costs, yet the book still holds them at a mean allocation of 0.11 and 0.24.
findings.F4: On hour-0 bars split in three by the size of the hour's move against each coin's median move, the fade earned +0.06 % (t 0.63, 2,059 cases) on small moves with raised 24-hour volatility. On large moves with raised volatility it earned +0.66 % (t 5.92, 3,358 cases). Raised volatility pays only when the settlement-hour move itself is large.
findings.F5: By quintile of the volatility ratio (about 3,087 cases each), the fade earned +0.08 % (t 0.93) in the lowest quintile, rising to +0.43 % (t 3.90) in the highest. The lowest-ratio fifth earns well under the 0.19 % cost.
findings.F6: The short side earned +0.17 % per case (t 3.13, 8,491 cases), below the cost of a trade; the long side earned +0.44 % (t 8.08, 8,532 cases). The shorts that lose are those against the coin's 7-day trend (a rise in the settlement hour while the 7-day return is negative): +0.07 % (t 0.86, 4,304 cases). Shorts with the 7-day trend earned +0.31 % (t 3.75, 3,681 cases).
findings.F7: Across all sides, fades that agree with the 7-day trend earned +0.39 % per case (t 7.12, 7,531 cases), against +0.20 % (t 3.51, 8,478) for fades against it. The 7-day trend alone, followed over the next 24 hours from the 00:00 bar, earns only +0.06 % to +0.10 % (t 0.99 to 1.52, about 5,400 cases per tercile). It is therefore not an effect of its own, but the brief's own reading of the crowded side: a settlement hour that moves against the recent trend recovers in the trend's direction.

ideas.idea: The larger a coin's 1-hour return in the first hour after the 00:00 UTC funding settlement relative to its 24-hour volatility, the more its return over the next 24 hours runs the opposite way, and more so the higher its 24-hour volatility stands against its 30-day volatility, the more so the further that hour's move runs against the coin's 7-day return.
ideas.consequence: A trader would fade the settlement-hour shock mainly when it pushed the coin against its week's trend, the crowded side's pre-payment exit, and would refuse the shorts that fight a falling week, which carry the book's losses for no gain.
ideas.name: settlement fade against weekly trend

ideas.idea: The larger a coin's 1-hour return in the first hour after the 00:00 UTC funding settlement relative to its 24-hour volatility, the more its return over the next 24 hours runs the opposite way, and more so the higher its 24-hour volatility stands against its 30-day volatility, with the reversal growing faster than the shock itself so that the largest settlement-hour moves carry most of the 24-hour give-back.
ideas.consequence: A trader would put nearly all the position on the largest settlement-hour shocks in raised volatility and stay out of the market on ordinary days, cutting the always-in exposure that builds the deep falls.
ideas.name: large settlement shocks reverse most
